segments.en: Early morning on the lake, and fishermen are paddling home in dugout canoes, their nets full of silver fish. This is Malawi, a long, narrow country that people call the Warm Heart of Africa.
Lake Malawi fills much of the country's eastern side. It is so vast it looks like a sea, with sandy beaches and rolling waves, yet the water is fresh.

Beneath the surface swim hundreds of kinds of cichlids, small fish in electric blue, yellow and orange, and many of them are found nowhere else in the world. At Cape Maclear, you can snorkel right among them.
The nickname comes from the people. Strangers are greeted with a smile and a cheerful Moni, which means hello in Chichewa, the most widely spoken language alongside English.

Greetings matter here. Before getting down to business, people ask how you slept and how your family is, and it is polite to give and receive things with both hands, or with your right hand supported by your left.
The heart of every meal is nsima, a thick maize porridge. You roll a little ball of it in your right hand and dip it into relish, perhaps beans, pumpkin leaves, or chambo, the lake's most loved fish.
The capital, Lilongwe, is a green and spread-out city, while Blantyre in the south is the old trading hub, named after the Scottish town where the explorer David Livingstone was born.
Rising out of the southern plains, Mount Mulanje is a huge granite massif with misty forests, waterfalls and cool streams, and hikers sleep in mountain huts along the trails.
Around Thyolo and Mulanje, tea estates roll out like bright green carpets, and pickers move between the bushes with baskets on their backs.
In the far north, the Nyika Plateau is a high world of rolling grassland, where zebra and antelope graze and wild orchids bloom after the rains.
Along the Shire River in Liwonde National Park, boats glide past hippos and crocodiles, while elephants wander down to the water's edge to drink.

Among the Chewa people, dancers perform Gule Wamkulu, the great dance, wearing carved and painted masks that represent spirits, animals and ancestors. It is honoured by UNESCO as part of the world's living heritage.
In the afternoons, football fills every dusty pitch, and the whole country cheers for the national team, known as the Flames.
As the sun sets gold over the water, Malawians will wish you a safe journey. Across the lake and to the south, Mozambique is waiting.
